title: COLDCARD Wallet Flaw Lets Hackers Drain $89 Million in Bitcoin Without Touching a Device
excerpt: A random number generator bug in the popular hardware wallet made recovery phrases predictable, allowing attackers to steal over 1,000 bitcoin from 1,196 wallets in 41 minutes. Coinkite urges all users to migrate funds immediately.
body:
• A firmware bug in Coldcard hardware wallets weakened the random number generator used to create recovery phrases, making them predictable to sophisticated attackers.
  • Galaxy Research traced at least three waves of attacks beginning July 30, with estimated total losses reaching $89 million across more than 1,200 wallets.
  • Coinkite has released a firmware update but warns it does not fix seeds already generated — users must create entirely new wallets and transfer their bitcoin.
  • Block's security team published the advisory and says attacks are ongoing, prompting urgent calls across the crypto industry to migrate funds.

Attackers exploited a firmware flaw in Coldcard, one of the most trusted Bitcoin hardware wallets, to drain roughly $89 million in cryptocurrency — all without physically accessing any of the targeted devices. The attack, first reported by Forbes on August 2 and confirmed through blockchain analysis by Galaxy Research, marks one of the largest security failures in the hardware wallet industry.

Galaxy's researchers traced the initial wave to July 30, when more than 1,000 bitcoin were siphoned from 1,196 digital wallets in just 41 minutes. Two additional suspected waves of suspicious activity were later identified, pushing estimated losses to nearly $89 million. Galaxy cautioned that its figures are based on blockchain analysis and that not every affected wallet has been confirmed as a Coldcard-generated address.

The Flaw: Predictable Recovery Phrases

According to a security advisory from Block's Bitcoin Engineering and Security team, a coding error in certain firmware versions weakened Coldcard's random number generator — the component responsible for producing the 12- or 24-word recovery phrases that serve as a wallet's master key.

https://x.com/cyrilXBT/status/2084200109903069368

The bug made some recovery phrases predictable enough for sophisticated attackers to reconstruct without ever handling the physical device. Because the weakness resides in the seed itself, not the hardware, transferring a compromised seed to another wallet provides no protection.

"Updating the firmware does not repair a seed that was generated by affected firmware. A new seed must be generated and the funds migrated to the new wallet."

— Coinkite, security advisory

Block emphasized that none of its own products or customers were affected. The company said it published its findings after working with anonymous security researchers and receiving reports directly from Coldcard users, and warned that attacks are ongoing.

Coinkite's Response and Industry Alarm

Canadian manufacturer Coinkite, which builds the Coldcard line, released a firmware patch to prevent the flaw from affecting newly generated wallets. But the company made clear that existing users cannot simply update and move on. Anyone who created a recovery phrase using affected firmware must generate a brand-new seed with the patched software and move every satoshi to the freshly secured wallet.

Coinkite CEO Rodolfo Novak issued a public apology on X: "I'm sorry and I'm devastated. Our team is heartbroken about yesterday's news." He urged customers to act before doing anything else. "If you generated a seed using a Coldcard wallet, move your funds now, using our updated best practices, before reading further," Novak wrote.

"If you know anyone who owns a Coldcard, please make sure they see this. Some affected users may not be watching social media right now, and every hour matters."

— Rodolfo Novak, Coinkite CEO

The warning rippled through the cryptocurrency community. Jan3 CEO Samson Mow posted on X urging users to migrate immediately: "If you're using a COLDCARD, any version firmware or MK, migrate your funds immediately... Attacks are ongoing so do it quickly."

Coinkite initially focused its warning on older Coldcard models but has since expanded the list to include additional devices and firmware versions. Users who generated their recovery phrases using at least 50 private dice rolls are not affected by this specific vulnerability, the company said, though it recommended that anyone uncertain about their setup create a new seed as a precaution.

Broader Implications for Crypto Security

The incident strikes at a foundational promise of hardware wallets: that keeping bitcoin offline makes it safe. Coldcard's air-gapped design was considered among the most secure in the industry, favoured by bitcoin maximalists who prioritize self-custody over exchange-based storage. The revelation that a firmware-level RNG flaw could undermine that security — silently and at scale — raises uncomfortable questions about the supply-chain integrity of crypto hardware.

Separately, developers of Block's Bitkey wallet said they are investigating a different reported issue involving their product but described the risk as minimal. "Our assessment is this presents no risk of remote drains or immediate funds loss," Bitkey developer Clay Garrett wrote on X.

What's Next

Novak said Coinkite is still working to determine the full scope of affected users and plans to publish a detailed technical explanation once its investigation is complete. The company has pledged to assist affected customers with police reports and insurance claims, and is cooperating with blockchain investigators and law enforcement agencies.

For Indian crypto investors — many of whom adopted hardware wallets after India's 2022 tax reforms pushed self-custody over exchange storage — the episode is a reminder that "offline" does not always mean "safe." Security researchers and industry leaders are urging anyone holding bitcoin in any Coldcard wallet to verify their seed generation method and migrate funds without delay.
